analysis.one_liner: Sets federal minimum health and safety standards for residential teen treatment programs to prevent child abuse.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 318-103, but the Senate never voted, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required residential programs for troubled teens — wilderness camps, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools, and behavior modification programs — to meet federal minimum standards banning abuse, withholding of food and medical care, and excessive restraints and seclusion. It created a national hotline, public websites listing program violations and child deaths, civil fines up to $50,000 per violation, criminal background checks for all staff, and Justice Department enforcement. The House passed it by a wide margin the day after it was introduced, but the Senate referred it to committee and never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Teenagers placed in residential treatment programs — wilderness camps, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools, and behavior modification facilities — and their parents, who would gain federal safety standards, background checks on staff, a hotline to report abuse, and public disclosure of program violations and child deaths.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Teens in residential programs and their parents

how_it_helps.text: Bans child abuse and neglect, and prohibits withholding food, water, shelter, or medical care as discipline at covered residential programs [S4].

Requires criminal background checks, including FBI fingerprint checks and sex-offender registry searches, for every staff member and volunteer with contact with children, disqualifying anyone convicted of child abuse, violent crimes, or sexual offenses [S4].
Limits physical and mechanical restraints and seclusion to the same rules that apply to non-medical community children's facilities [S4].

Creates a national toll-free hotline for abuse complaints, with a 30-day federal investigation requirement, and public websites disclosing each program's violations, penalties, and any deaths of children in its care [S4].
Authorizes civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation and Justice Department lawsuits when violations are not remedied [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of residential teen programs — wilderness therapy companies, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools, and behavior modification operators — who would face federal standards, inspections, public disclosure of violations and deaths, and civil fines. Federal appropriations of $15 million a year plus additional child-abuse-prevention grant money would be spent on oversight [S4].

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes a new federal regulatory layer over programs that many states already license, raising compliance costs for operators, and small private programs might close or raise prices rather than meet the standards — potentially reducing treatment options for families [S4].
It ties federal child-abuse-prevention grant money to states adopting the standards, which critics can fairly call federal pressure on state licensing decisions [S4].

Enforcement depends heavily on HHS rulemaking and staffing within fixed deadlines (interim rules within 180 days), an aggressive timeline that could strain the agency and invite implementation delays or legal challenges [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed documented abuse at residential teen programs with measures aimed directly at the harms: background checks, bans on deprivation and restraint, disclosure of deaths and violations, and fines. The main costs are compliance burdens on operators and a modest federal spending authorization, plus some overlap with state licensing. Against the risk of abuse and death of children in unregulated programs, the tradeoff strongly favors the bill; the Republican members who voted no were objecting to the federal role rather than defending abuse, but the practical effect of the Senate's inaction was that no standards took effect.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it under a fast-track procedure the day after introduction, but the Senate sent it to its health committee, which never brought it to a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced June 24, 2008, and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee [S6].
The next day, Rep. George Miller moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill — a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority and typically used for noncontroversial bills [S6].
The House passed it 318-103 (Roll no. 459): all 235 Democrats present voted yes, and 89 of 199 Republicans voted yes [S7].

The Senate received the bill on June 26, 2008, and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no further action was recorded before the 110th Congress ended January 3, 2009 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of residential teen programs — wilderness camps, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools, and behavior modification facilities — which remained without federal safety standards, public disclosure of violations and deaths, or federal penalties.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Operators of unregulated residential teen programs

industries.industry: Residential teen treatment programs (wilderness therapy, boot camps, therapeutic boarding schools, behavior modification facilities)
industries.note: The bill would have subjected these operators to federal minimum standards, background checks, unannounced inspections, public disclosure of violations and child deaths, and fines up to $50,000 per violation. Their interest in remaining outside federal oversight ran against the safety of the children they housed. Because the bill died, they remained unregulated at the federal level.
